findings.quote: Its centrepiece, the clitoris, is a densely innervated erectile organ homologous with the penis, most of which lies beneath the surface.
findings.explanation: The relative clause 'most of which lies beneath the surface' attaches to the nearest noun, 'the penis', so the opening description of a female-anatomy page can be read as saying that the penis mostly lies beneath the surface. The writer means the clitoris. The homology itself is correct, but a male structure becomes the grammatical subject of the page's first description, which fits the user complaint about male anatomy on this page.
findings.suggestedFix: Keep the clitoris as the only subject and move the comparison out of the intro: 'Its centrepiece, the clitoris, is a densely innervated erectile organ, most of which lies beneath the surface.' State the penile homology once, in the development section.

findings.quote: The glottis consists of the vestibular folds, the true vocal folds and the space between them.
findings.explanation: The same paragraph defines the supraglottis as the region above the vocal folds and the glottis as the region at their level, and then says the vestibular (false) folds lie above the true folds. By that definition, and in standard clinical anatomy and cancer staging (supraglottic versus glottic tumours), the vestibular folds are supraglottic; the glottis is the true vocal folds plus the rima glottidis. The sentence may follow a simplified textbook wording.
findings.suggestedFix: The glottis consists of the true vocal folds and the space between them (the rima glottidis); the vestibular folds belong to the supraglottis.

findings.quote: The skeleton of the larynx consists of three unpaired midline cartilages and four pairs of smaller cartilages.
findings.explanation: The larynx has nine cartilages: three unpaired (epiglottis, thyroid, cricoid) and three paired (arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform). The page's own key fact 'Paired cartilages' lists exactly those three pairs, and the paragraph goes on to name only arytenoids and corniculates, so 'four pairs' is a miscount that contradicts the key facts.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to 'three pairs of smaller cartilages (arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform)'.

findings.quote: Arterial blood reaches the cerebellum mainly through the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) and the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA)
findings.explanation: The cerebellum has three paired arteries, all from the vertebrobasilar system: the superior cerebellar artery (SCA, from the basilar artery), AICA and PICA. The SCA supplies the superior surface, the upper vermis, the deep nuclei including the dentate, and the superior peduncle, and it is missing entirely, both here and in the key fact 'Blood supply' ('Mainly the posterior inferior and anterior inferior cerebellar arteries'). AICA has the smallest territory of the three, so 'mainly PICA and AICA' is wrong, and a superior cerebellar artery infarct (ipsilateral limb ataxia, dysarthria) cannot be understood from this page.
findings.suggestedFix: Name all three arteries with a one-line territory each (SCA: superior surface and deep nuclei; AICA: anterior-inferior surface and the labyrinthine artery; PICA: inferior surface and lateral medulla) and drop 'mainly' in both the key fact and the section.

findings.quote: From the same genital tubercle, folds and swellings that form the penis and scrotum
findings.explanation: Under the label 'Development' on a vulva page, the key-facts panel names only the penis and scrotum, so a reader scanning it sees male anatomy and no female structure; it never says what the vulva itself develops from and can be read as if the vulva forms the penis and scrotum. As a statement of shared origin it is accurate. The page carries more male-anatomy detail that is correct but off-topic for a vulva: penile urethra, scrotum, bulbourethral glands, prostate, vaginoplasty and metoidioplasty in 'Function and development'; the phalloplasty/neophallus sentence in 'Innervation'; the neoclitoris from the glans of the penis in 'Changes across life'.
findings.suggestedFix: Make the female structures the subject: 'Develops from the genital tubercle, urogenital folds and labioscrotal swellings (clitoris, labia minora, labia majora); in a male-typical pathway the same tissues form the penis and scrotum.' Consider moving the phalloplasty sentence in Innervation, and most surgical homology detail, to the neophallus and neovagina pages.

findings.quote: The retina and optic disc are supplied by fine branches of the arteries entering the back of the eye, including the short posterior ciliary arteries that also supply the ciliary processes.
findings.explanation: The short posterior ciliary arteries supply the choroid and the optic nerve head; the ciliary body and its processes are supplied by the long posterior and anterior ciliary arteries (major arterial circle of the iris). The sentence also never names the central retinal artery (a branch of the ophthalmic artery), which supplies the inner retina, whose branches are the vessels seen with the ophthalmoscope in the next sentence, and whose occlusion causes sudden painless loss of vision in one eye.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite: 'The inner retina is supplied by the central retinal artery, a branch of the ophthalmic artery; the outer retina and optic nerve head by the choroidal circulation (short posterior ciliary arteries); the ciliary body by the long posterior and anterior ciliary arteries.'

findings.quote: Brainstem infarcts account for nearly one-third of all ischaemic strokes
findings.explanation: Posterior-circulation infarcts as a whole (brainstem, cerebellum, thalamus and occipital lobe together) are usually put at about a fifth to a quarter of ischaemic strokes, so brainstem infarcts alone are well under a third. The same figure is repeated in the key fact 'Clinical'. None of the cited references (a brain-stem-death leaflet, MedlinePlus, OpenStax and StatPearls anatomy chapters) is likely to give stroke epidemiology.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the fraction, or replace it with 'posterior-circulation strokes, which include brainstem infarcts, make up roughly a fifth to a quarter of ischaemic strokes' with a stroke-epidemiology source; change the key fact to match.

findings.quote: Front of the neck, opposite the third to seventh cervical vertebrae, held in place by muscles and ligaments
findings.explanation: In adults the larynx lies opposite C3 to C6: the hyoid is at C3 and the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, where the trachea begins, is at C6. C7 lies below the larynx. The body text repeats the error ('at the level of the third to seventh cervical vertebrae' in 'Location and relations').
findings.suggestedFix: Change both to 'third to sixth cervical vertebrae'.

findings.quote: All of these intrinsic muscles are supplied by the vagus nerve, mainly through its recurrent laryngeal branch
findings.explanation: Incomplete nerve supply that hides a real exception: cricothyroid, one of the muscles just listed, is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, not the recurrent laryngeal nerve, and sensation is split (internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve above the vocal folds, recurrent laryngeal nerve below). Injury to the external branch (for example in thyroid surgery) causes voice fatigue and loss of pitch range rather than the hoarseness of recurrent laryngeal palsy. The key fact 'Nerve supply' repeats the simplification, and the page names no laryngeal artery (superior laryngeal from the superior thyroid artery, inferior laryngeal from the inferior thyroid artery).
findings.suggestedFix: State that every intrinsic muscle except cricothyroid is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve and cricothyroid by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve; add the sensory split and one sentence naming the superior and inferior laryngeal arteries.

findings.quote: The right and left vagal trunks lie on the lower oesophagus and pass with it through the hiatus
findings.explanation: At the lower oesophagus the two vagi have recombined in the oesophageal plexus and continue as the anterior vagal trunk (mainly left vagus) and the posterior vagal trunk (mainly right vagus), not as right and left trunks. This matters for vagotomy and hiatal surgery.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'the anterior and posterior vagal trunks (formed mainly from the left and right vagus nerves)'.

findings.quote: in the upper two-thirds the fibres are a mixture of skeletal and smooth muscle, the skeletal fibres fading out in the lower third
findings.explanation: The usual description (and, to my recollection, the cited OpenStax chapter) is in thirds: upper third skeletal muscle, middle third a mixture, lower third smooth muscle only. The page makes the whole upper two-thirds 'mixed', which is wrong for the top third next to the cricopharyngeus, where the muscle is almost wholly skeletal. The key fact 'Muscle' repeats the two-thirds wording.
findings.suggestedFix: Upper third skeletal, middle third a mixture of skeletal and smooth, lower third smooth only; change the key fact to match.

findings.quote: At every level there are three layers: a dorsal tectum, a central tegmentum and a ventral basis carrying the descending tracts.
findings.explanation: The tectum (the roof, carrying the colliculi) is a midbrain structure. The pons and medulla have a tegmentum and a basis (basilar pons; pyramids) but no tectum; their dorsal surface forms the floor of the fourth ventricle beneath the cerebellum. 'At each level' in the key fact 'Internal layers' repeats the over-generalisation.
findings.suggestedFix: Say that the midbrain has a tectum, tegmentum and basis, and that the pons and medulla have a tegmentum and a basis; change the key fact to match.

findings.quote: a shallow depression bounded in front by the external iliac vessels and behind by the internal iliac vessels and the ureter
findings.explanation: In standard descriptions the ovarian fossa is bounded above by the external iliac vessels, in front by the obliterated umbilical artery (medial umbilical ligament), and behind by the ureter and internal iliac artery. The external iliac vessels are its upper boundary, not the anterior one, and the usual anterior landmark is missing. A simplification rather than a serious error.
findings.suggestedFix: 'bounded above by the external iliac vessels, in front by the obliterated umbilical artery and behind by the ureter and the internal iliac vessels'.

findings.quote: A pudendal nerve block at the ischial spine anaesthetises the vulva and lower vagina for an instrumental birth or the repair of a tear
findings.explanation: The same section says the mons and the front of the labia majora are supplied by the ilioinguinal and genitofemoral nerves (L1-L2), which a pudendal block does not reach, so the block does not numb the whole vulva. It numbs the perineum, posterior vulva and lower vagina. The vagina page words this correctly ('numbs the lower vagina and perineum'). Many obstetric texts use the looser phrase, hence medium confidence.
findings.suggestedFix: Say it anaesthetises the perineum, posterior vulva and lower vagina, and that the front of the vulva has a separate supply and may need local infiltration.

findings.quote: causing combinations of double vision, vertigo, facial weakness, difficulty swallowing and limb weakness; MRI shows them best.
findings.explanation: The page describes how brainstem stroke presents but gives the reader no action; sudden double vision, vertigo, facial droop, swallowing difficulty or limb weakness is a 999 situation. The cerebellum page has the same gap: it says 'cerebellar strokes and tumours are treated as emergencies' but never says what a reader with sudden unsteadiness, vertigo and headache should do.
findings.suggestedFix: Add one sentence on both pages: sudden vertigo, double vision, slurred speech, facial droop, limb weakness, or unsteadiness with a severe headache may be a stroke and needs a 999 call straight away (NHS FAST advice).

findings.quote: Nosebleeds are managed by sitting forward and pinching the soft part of the nose; persistent bleeding is cauterised or packed.
findings.explanation: First-aid content with no duration and no escalation advice. Usual NHS advice is to pinch the soft part for about 10 to 15 minutes and to seek urgent help if bleeding is heavy or does not stop, follows a head injury, or the person takes anticoagulants or has difficulty breathing. 'Persistent' is not defined, so a reader cannot tell when to go to A&E.
findings.suggestedFix: Add the pinching time and one line saying that heavy bleeding, bleeding that continues after 10 to 15 minutes of pressure, or bleeding after a head injury or on blood thinners needs urgent medical help.

findings.quote: Polycystic ovary syndrome is diagnosed when two of three features are present: irregular or absent ovulation, clinical or biochemical excess androgen, and many small follicles on ultrasound. Scanning is not needed when the other two features are present, and other causes must first be excluded.
findings.explanation: The criteria and the exception for scanning match the Rotterdam/international guideline as I know it, but none of the five listed references covers PCOS (OpenStax ovarian chapter, Society for Endocrinology ovary page, NHS ovarian cyst, NHS ovarian cancer, NHS menopause). The same is true of the ectopic pregnancy lines (ampulla, urgent assessment) and of the paragraph on testosterone, ovulation and contraception in trans men and non-binary people in 'Changes across life'.
findings.suggestedFix: Add the NHS PCOS and ectopic pregnancy pages and a gender-affirming hormone source, or trim the unreferenced detail.

findings.quote: Lichen sclerosus, a chronic inflammatory skin condition, causes itch, white thinned skin and scarring; it is treated with steroid ointment and is kept under review, because a small number of people with it go on to develop vulval cancer
findings.explanation: The four references are two OpenStax chapters, the generic NHS sexual health hub and the NHS menopause page. None covers lichen sclerosus, Bartholin's cyst and abscess, vulval cancer, vulvodynia or female genital mutilation, and the detailed nerve supply (ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, posterior femoral cutaneous, cavernous nerves) is not at that level in OpenStax either. The statements are accurate as far as I know, but a reader cannot check them.
findings.suggestedFix: Add NHS pages for lichen sclerosus, Bartholin's cyst, vulval cancer, vulvodynia and FGM, plus an anatomy source for the nerve supply, or trim the unreferenced clinical lines.

findings.quote: Trans men and non-binary people taking testosterone can develop similar atrophy, because the therapy suppresses ovarian oestrogen production, and topical vaginal oestrogen can be used alongside testosterone without reversing masculinising effects.
findings.explanation: A prescribing-type statement about combining vaginal oestrogen with testosterone is not supported by any of the four references on this page (OpenStax, NHS prolapse, NHS menopause, NHS UTIs); the gender-affirming guideline cited on the pelvic floor page is not listed here. The claim is plausible (low systemic absorption) but is a clinical judgement that needs a source. The neovagina sentence about 'a lifelong dilation routine' is also unreferenced on this page.
findings.suggestedFix: Cite the UCSF or WPATH guidance on this page, or soften to 'topical vaginal oestrogen is sometimes prescribed alongside testosterone; this is a decision for the prescriber'.

findings.quote: (one of them, on the right, often from a branch of the arch)
findings.explanation: The usual textbook origin of the right bronchial artery is the right third posterior intercostal artery (the intercostobronchial trunk) or the upper left bronchial artery, both from the descending thoracic aorta at about T5 to T6; an origin from the aortic arch is a variant, not 'often'. Not certain: the wording may derive from the structure list ('Bronchial branch of arch of aorta'), and the cited StatPearls chapters may describe variants.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'usually one right and two left, arising from the descending thoracic aorta (the right often via the intercostobronchial trunk)', or delete the parenthesis.

notes: No web access used. All 15 entities (ids 15 to 29) read in full; 20 findings, none dropped for the cap, none rated high. VULVA: every male-anatomy passage is factually correct (intro homology; Development key fact; 'Function and development': penis, penile urethra, scrotum, bulbourethral glands, prostate, metoidioplasty; 'Innervation': phalloplasty sentence; 'Changes across life': neoclitoris from the penile glans), so the complaint is about wording and placement, not error. The phalloplasty sentence in Innervation is the least relevant to a vulva and could move to the neophallus page. The vulva's nerve supply is otherwise complete and correct (pudendal S2-S4 with posterior labial and dorsal clitoral nerves; ilioinguinal and genitofemoral to the mons and anterior labia; perineal branch of the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve; cavernous nerves); the block sentence is the only slip. The note that the 3D atlas base body is male comes from the page template (anatomy/anatomy.js), not from the entity text. Seen but not reported (not confident, or trivial): diaphragm 'C3 to C5, with a contribution from C6' (standard teaching is C3 to C5, with C6 only via an accessory phrenic nerve; worth a quick check); diaphragm hiatus-hernia symptom list names chest pain and difficulty swallowing with no 'get assessed' caution; vagina says the upper three-quarters is autonomic but the lower third carries most sensation (thirds versus quarters); pelvic floor 'which also supplies the external urethral sphincter' can be read as the inferior rectal branch (it is the perineal branch); tongue 'a complete cure is possible in most cases' could be softened; the brainstem-death text (two senior doctors, two sets of tests) follows the 2008 UK code of practice, so check it against the current code (I could not confirm whether it has been revised); eye 'Muscles and nerves' names no nerves (III, IV, VI, V1) and the larynx and nose pages name no arteries; trachea: right-sided predominance of inhaled objects is an adult finding and is less marked in young children, whom the same page stresses.
